qs.q: What is the characteristic hormonal profile found in Turner syndrome due to gonadal dysgenesis?
o: Low follicle-stimulating hormone, low luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen
Normal gonadotropin levels with low oestrogen and normal feedback
High prolactin with suppressed gonadotropins and normal oestrogen
High follicle-stimulating hormone, high luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen
qs.e: Turner syndrome features streak gonads causing primary ovarian failure, which yields very high gonadotropins due to a lack of negative feedback, alongside low oestrogen. This hypergonadotropic hypogonadism results in primary amenorrhea.

qs.q: An infant with Turner syndrome is found to have a large, soft, translucent mass in the left neck. Histologic examination reveals dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium. What is the standard designation for this anomaly?
qs.e: Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas typically found in the head and neck region of children, frequently associated with Turner syndrome. Simple lymphangiomas and hemangiomas lack these large, macroscopic cystic spaces.

qs.q: Which of the following interventions is specifically indicated for the management of children with growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, or chronic kidney disease who fail to catch up in height?
o: Daily growth hormone replacement therapy injections
Therapeutic F-75 milk formulas given indefinitely
qs.e: Growth hormone therapy via daily injection is used for growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney disease, Prader-Willi syndrome, and short children born small for gestational age. Corticosteroids can actually suppress growth rather than treat these conditions.

qs.q: A newborn presents with a congenital heart defect associated with Turner syndrome. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Turner syndrome is classically associated with coarctation of the aorta and a bicuspid aortic valve. Atrioventricular septal defect is more commonly linked with Trisomy 21.

qs.q: NOT a clinical feature of Turner syndrome?
qs.e: Turner syndrome affects females (45,X) — there are no testes. The correct gonadal finding is streak ovaries.

qs.q: What is the typical hormonal pattern in Turner syndrome (45,X0)?
o: Normal follicle-stimulating hormone, normal luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen
Low follicle-stimulating hormone, low luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen
High prolactin concentration, low follicle-stimulating hormone
High follicle-stimulating hormone, high luteinizing hormone, low oestrogen
qs.e: Turner syndrome is associated with streak gonads, resulting in primary ovarian failure. This leads to very high FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) and low oestrogen, causing primary amenorrhea.

qs.q: Turner syndrome (45,X0) shows which hormonal pattern?
o: High FSH, high LH, low oestrogen
Low FSH, low LH, low oestrogen
qs.e: Turner syndrome: streak gonads → primary ovarian failure → very high FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), low oestrogen, primary amenorrhoea. Short stature, webbed neck, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of aorta.

qs.q: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes infertility because of
o: Premature ovarian failure — streak gonads → primary amenorrhea + elevated FSH/LH
qs.e: Turner syndrome: 45,X (or mosaic). Streak gonads (fibrous tissue replacing ovaries) → no estrogen/progesterone → no negative feedback → elevated FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Features: short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, coarctation of aorta, horseshoe kidney. Requires estrogen replacement for puberty induction and bone protection.
